chapters.title: Chapter 6: Putting Forex Knowledge to Work

lessons.title: How Rupee Moves Hit Your Portfolio: IT Stocks, Oil Companies and US Investments

children.text: Ananya, a 34-year-old product manager in Pune, has never traded a currency contract in her life. Yet her portfolio is full of rupee bets. She owns shares of large IT services companies, a stake in an oil marketing company, a pharma exporter, and a US index fund bought through LRS. As the rupee weakened from about 89.9 to 95.5 per dollar in 2026, some of those holdings quietly gained from the currency while others were squeezed by it. Most investors never notice this. This lesson shows you which parts of an Indian portfolio win and lose when the rupee moves, how to measure the effect on IT margins and on foreign investments, and how to check whether your own portfolio is making a currency bet you never intended.

body.text: The rupee is a hidden factor in almost every Indian portfolio. Businesses that earn in dollars and spend in rupees gain when the rupee weakens. Businesses that earn in rupees and pay in dollars get hurt. And every foreign investment you own carries the exchange rate as a second, separate source of return.

body.title: The margin tailwind
body.prompt: Using a rule of thumb of 35 basis points of operating margin for every 1% fall in the rupee, how many percentage points would a 4% rupee depreciation add to an IT company's operating margin, all else equal?
body.explanation: 4 × 35 basis points = 140 basis points, which is 1.40 percentage points. A company at a 21% operating margin would move to about 22.4% from the currency alone, before any change in pricing, wages or demand.

body.title: Why the real effect is smaller than simple arithmetic suggests

children.text: Take a simplified IT company with $1 billion of revenue at USD/INR 90.00, or ₹9,000 crore, and ₹7,110 crore of costs, all in rupees. Operating profit is ₹1,890 crore, a 21% margin. If USD/INR rises 5% to 94.50, revenue becomes ₹9,450 crore while costs stay at ₹7,110 crore. Operating profit jumps to ₹2,340 crore, a margin of about 24.8%, a gain of 3.76 percentage points.

Real companies see much less, which is why analysts use 30 to 40 basis points per 1% rather than the roughly 75 basis points this toy example implies. Part of their cost base is abroad, such as onsite employees and subcontractors paid in dollars. They hedge future revenue with forwards, so today's rate reaches the income statement only gradually. And clients who know the rupee has weakened push for price cuts at contract renewals, passing some of the benefit back.

body.text: A currency tailwind is not growth. In 2022, the rupee fell about 10%, yet the Nifty IT index fell more than 25% as global technology valuations dropped and investors worried about US clients cutting spending. The currency lifts margins at the edges. Deal wins, client budgets and valuations decide the share price. Never buy an IT stock only because the rupee is falling.

children.text: Oil Companies, Airlines and Importers: The Rupee Losers

The mirror image is any company that pays in dollars and earns in rupees. Oil marketing companies such as Indian Oil, BPCL and HPCL buy crude and some products priced in dollars and sell petrol, diesel and LPG in rupees. When pump prices are not revised in step with costs, a weaker rupee and higher crude hit their margins together. Airlines face the same squeeze: jet fuel is priced off global benchmarks, and aircraft leases and maintenance are largely linked to the dollar, while most tickets are sold in rupees. Importers of electronics, machinery and components either raise prices, accept thinner margins or lose customers.

body.title: Who benefits from a rupee rally?
body.question: If the rupee strengthens sharply, as it did on 2 April 2026, which business is most likely to see an immediate benefit to its margins?
options: An IT services company billing US clients
A pharma company selling generics in the US
An airline paying dollar-linked fuel and lease costs
A textile exporter selling to European buyers
body.explanation: A stronger rupee cuts the rupee cost of dollar-linked expenses such as fuel and leases, which helps the airline. The other three earn in foreign currency and lose some rupee revenue when the rupee strengthens.

children.text: US Investments: The Second Return You Did Not Choose

When you buy a US index fund, directly under LRS or through an Indian international fund of funds, your rupee return depends on two things: how the investment performs in dollars, and how USD/INR moves while you hold it. A weaker rupee adds to your return. A stronger rupee subtracts from it. The two combine by multiplication, not simple addition.

body.caption: The change in USD/INR is positive when the rupee weakens
S&P 500 price returns for an Indian investor (approximate, ignoring dividends, costs and taxes)

children.text: In 2022, US stocks fell hard, but the rupee's slide cushioned Indian investors, halving the loss in rupee terms. That is the diversification benefit of holding foreign assets: the rupee tends to weaken during global stress, which is often when foreign stocks are falling too. The same effect works against you when the rupee rallies.

body.title: Ananya's US fund in rupees
body.prompt: Ananya's US index fund rises 8% in dollar terms over a period in which USD/INR moves from 89.90 to 95.50. What is her return in rupees? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: Change in USD/INR = 95.50 ÷ 89.90 minus 1 = 6.23%. Rupee return = 1.08 × 1.0623 minus 1 = 14.73%. Simply adding 8% and 6.23% gives 14.23%, which understates the result because the currency gain also applies to the investment gain.

body.text: Do not treat past rupee depreciation as a guaranteed bonus on foreign investments. The rupee's long-run drift has been weaker, but it can rally sharply, as it did in April 2026, and a few years of a stable or stronger rupee can erase a large part of the expected currency boost. Foreign investing also brings extra costs: spreads on converting rupees, TCS above the LRS threshold, fund expenses and different tax treatment. Invest abroad for diversification, not to bet on the rupee.

children.text: About 55% of Ananya's portfolio benefits directly from a weaker rupee, and only 10% is hurt by it. Without planning it, she has a large bet that the rupee keeps weakening. That may suit her, since her future expenses are in rupees and some dollar exposure diversifies her salary. But she should know it is there, because a sustained rupee rally would hit more than half her holdings at once.

body.title: Should Ananya sell her US fund?
body.scenario: After the rupee's slide to 95.5, a friend tells Ananya: "The rupee has fallen too far and RBI is fighting it. The currency boost is over. Sell your US index fund and buy more IT stocks instead, since they also earn in dollars." Ananya holds her US fund for long-term diversification, and her goals, a home purchase in 10 years and retirement, are in rupees.
body.prompt: Evaluate her friend's advice. Consider what each holding is really exposed to, whether switching reduces or increases her rupee bet, and what a sensible approach would look like.
body.modelAnswer:
1. The advice is a short-term currency forecast. Nobody can reliably call the end of a rupee trend, and RBI smoothing volatility does not mean the rupee will reverse.
2. Switching does not remove the rupee bet. IT stocks also benefit from a weaker rupee and suffer when it strengthens, so the portfolio would stay about 55% rupee-sensitive, while becoming more concentrated in one Indian sector.
3. The US fund gives exposure to different companies, sectors and an economy that her Indian holdings do not. IT stocks are Indian businesses exposed to Indian costs, wage inflation and client pricing pressure. They are not a substitute for owning US companies.
4. Her goals are in rupees, so a moderate foreign allocation for diversification makes sense, but the total currency-sensitive share, around 55%, may be higher than she intended.
5. Sensible approach: decide a target foreign allocation, say 10% to 20%, and a limit on sector concentration based on her goals and risk tolerance; rebalance periodically back to those targets rather than reacting to rupee headlines; and judge each holding on its own business case, not on currency forecasts.

body.title: A currency audit of your portfolio
steps: List each holding and note whether it mainly earns in rupees or in foreign currency.
Note which holdings have large dollar costs or dollar debt.
Add up the share that gains and the share that loses from a weaker rupee.
Include foreign funds, US stocks and dollar deposits in the foreign currency share.
Ask whether that net currency tilt fits goals that are mostly in rupees.
Rebalance to planned allocations rather than chasing recent rupee moves.

body.title: The rupee return formula
body.textWithBlank: Rupee return = (1 + dollar return) × (1 + change in USD/INR) minus ___.
body.explanation: Multiplying the two growth factors and subtracting 1 gives the combined return, including the currency gain earned on the investment gain itself.

points: Companies that earn in dollars and spend in rupees, such as IT services and pharma exporters, usually gain margin when the rupee weakens.
Companies that earn in rupees and pay in dollars, such as oil marketers, airlines and importers, usually lose margin.
Analysts estimate IT operating margins rise about 30 to 40 basis points per 1% rupee depreciation, but hedging, onsite costs and client price cuts dilute the effect.
A currency tailwind is not a substitute for business growth: IT stocks still had a poor 2022 despite a weak rupee.
Foreign investments return (1 + dollar return) × (1 + change in USD/INR) minus 1. The rupee's slide cushioned Indian investors in the S&P 500's fall in 2022.
Many Indian portfolios carry a hidden bet on a weaker rupee. Measure it, decide whether it fits your rupee goals, and rebalance to plan instead of reacting to currency headlines.
